headline_en: Remittances pass USD 2 billion in 25 days
summary_en: Bangladeshis abroad sent USD 203 crore 29 lakh home in the first 25 days of October 2025, according to Bangladesh Bank. The article breaks the inflow down by bank type, gives the reasons bankers cite for higher inflows through legal channels, and reports the foreign exchange reserve.

facts.statement: Bangladeshis abroad sent USD 203 crore 29 lakh to Bangladesh in the first 25 days of October 2025.
Bangladeshis abroad sent a total of USD 268 crore 50 lakh in September 2025; the article says October 2025 remittances may end up lower than September.

In the first 25 days of October 2025 remittances came through state-owned banks USD 38 crore 46 lakh, two specialised banks USD 19 crore 70 lakh, private banks USD 144 crore 63 lakh and foreign banks USD 48 lakh 70 thousand.

Bank officials say remittance inflow through legal channels has risen since the fall of the Awami League government in August 2024, and the high dollar price also encourages sending through legal channels.
March 2025 set the record for remittances in a single month at USD 329 crore; since then no month has exceeded USD 300 crore (as of late October 2025).
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report citing Bangladesh Bank data

facts.statement: The reasons given for higher remittances are that illegal hundi business has shrunk as money laundering fell, and the dollar exchange rate in the banking channel is stable, so more money comes by the legal route.
Bangladesh's gross foreign exchange reserve stood at USD 32.10 billion on 22 October 2025; under the IMF's BPM-6 method it was USD 27.35 billion.

headline_en: Driven to New York by climate disaster at home, and fearing deportation there too
summary_en: A year-long Columbia Journalism Investigations and Documented investigation (republished by Prothom Alo) analysed more than 9 million US border-apprehension records from 2010 to 2024 and found that thousands of migrants who crossed the Mexico border into the United States came from areas hit repeatedly by storms, floods and droughts, including Feni and Noakhali in Bangladesh. It profiles three migrants in New York, including Hossain from Feni, who paid USD 41,000 and travelled nine months through 11 countries, applied for political asylum, and now fears deportation under the Trump administration. The article explains that US asylum has no provision protecting people fleeing climate disaster.

facts.statement: Hossain, a rice farmer from Feni, Bangladesh, left Bangladesh in February 2023 and crossed 11 countries by air and land over 9 months before surrendering to border officials in the US state of Arizona.
facts.source_in_article: Hossain, interviewed by CJI and Documented

facts.statement: Hossain from Feni sold his land and borrowed about USD 33,000 from relatives and friends, raising USD 41,000 in total for travel costs and the broker's fee for the journey to the United States via the Mexico border.
After Hossain surrendered to border officials in Arizona, they held him for three days in one room with 15 people; after release he moved to New York.

According to documents obtained, a legal organisation in Manhattan filed a political asylum application for Hossain in April 2024, based on his being a supporter of Bangladesh's opposition political party; the effect of climate-related floods on his income and livelihood is not admissible as a ground for asylum.
facts.source_in_article: documents obtained by CJI and Documented

facts.statement: While waiting for his hearing in the overloaded immigration court, Hossain received a work permit after seven months (the article does not say from which date the seven months are counted).

Hossain first worked as a kitchen helper in a local restaurant, then delivered food by bike on the streets of Brooklyn, and now works full time at a Bengali sweet shop and cafe in Kensington, Brooklyn ('Little Bangladesh'); he works six days a week and seven days during religious festivals, and shares a basement apartment with two roommates.

There is no specific provision in the United States protecting people who flee climate disasters, so such migrants face uncertainty over immigration; they had hoped to get asylum at the south-west border.

US President Donald Trump is stepping up operations to arrest, detain and deport migrants; the threat of deportation has spread panic among Bengalis in Brooklyn, and the streets of Kensington, once busy around 'Noakhali Deshi Bazar' and eateries such as 'Raj Mahal Restaurant + Sweets', have gone quiet.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers detained two Bangladeshis from Noakhali who were working in Buffalo, New York; the news spread quickly in Kensington, Brooklyn.

Hossain keeps copies of his asylum application and his court hearing notices in a plastic folder in his bedroom drawer, always within reach, and has put his lawyer's number on speed dial on his mobile phone in case ICE officers raid his home.

Hossain had hoped that once granted political asylum he could apply to bring his wife and daughter to him; he said that if he had known it was this hard now, he would not have come to the United States.

When Hossain's wife Sumaiya gave birth by caesarean in a Feni hospital in September 2022 he was handed a bill of USD 470 (about 57,500 taka) that he could not pay and had to borrow from relatives and a friend; his home had flooded five times in a decade and he could farm only one third of his land for several years.

In 2024 the worst flood in more than three decades hit Feni; Hossain's family home went under three feet of water and his wife and daughter had to move to a relative's house in Dhaka about 100 miles (160 km) away. He estimates rebuilding a home in Feni would cost about USD 45,000 (about 55 lakh taka).

Hossain said that because he joined opposition politics in Bangladesh, ruling-party members kept threatening him, while floods kept destroying his crops; together these forced him to leave. A friend advised him to go to Brooklyn because of its large Bangladeshi settlement, after he learned that many were getting asylum in the United States.
Border crossings from Bangladesh at the US-Mexico border rose 150 percent between 2019 and 2024.
facts.source_in_article: Columbia Journalism Investigations (CJI) and Documented analysis

facts.statement: In US border-apprehension records of Bangladeshis, Noakhali tops the districts of origin with more than 30 percent; more people from Bangladesh's coastal areas than from other areas migrated to the US southern border, and Feni town in disaster-prone Chattogram division is among the top 10 Bangladeshi towns from which the most people reached the US-Mexico border.
facts.source_in_article: Columbia Journalism Investigations (CJI) and Documented analysis

facts.statement: CJI and Documented found that among those apprehended in 2024 alone, more than 520 were born in Guatemala, about 350 in Senegal and about 100 in Bangladesh (as the article states, in the context of the climate-hit areas it studied).
facts.source_in_article: Columbia Journalism Investigations (CJI) and Documented analysis

facts.statement: An estimated 1 lakh (100,000) Bangladeshis live in New York City. Newly arrived Bangladeshi migrants first settle around Bangladeshi groceries and restaurants in Kensington, Brooklyn; most come from Bangladesh's coastal areas.
More than 237,000 migrants and asylum seekers have arrived in New York City since April 2022, straining the city's shelter system; local hotels and large tents are used for emergency housing.

A recent survey by New York City community organisation Desis Rising Up and Moving (DRUM) found 135 newly arrived Bangladeshi and other migrants who had been forced to leave their countries because of climate disasters.

Bangladesh, Guatemala and Senegal did not receive Temporary Protected Status (TPS) from the United States between 2019 and 2024. Migrants eligible for TPS because of natural disasters usually fall into the 'inadmissible' category in US border data.

In a WhatsApp voice note shared by a Bronx imam, a migrant just back from immigration court warned that officials are giving migrants only two weeks to submit all required documents before deciding whether they can stay in the United States.
facts.source_in_article: voice note from a West African migrants' WhatsApp group, shared by Imam Sheikh Tidiane Ndao

facts.statement: Griselda, a Guatemalan migrant in New York, said she once applied for asylum in the United States but one of the people helping her with it embezzled several thousand dollars from her, after which she could not trust the system enough to try again.
Griselda's workplace gave her a red card with detailed instructions on what to do if confronted by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers; it is the only document she has.

Human smugglers often posed as travel agents and made TikTok and Instagram videos (in the Wolof language for Senegalese viewers) promoting the journey to the United States as very comfortable and saying a US work permit and job are very easy to get; reels showed migrants entering the US via Nicaragua. One smuggler advertised arranging visas and air tickets and connected people to other smugglers on the way.
facts.source_in_article: Mohamed, Senegalese migrant; CJI and Documented report

facts.statement: Mohamed, a Senegalese migrant, said he was told that once he reached the United States 'everyone is equal before the law; no one can deport you'.

Mohamed, 45, a farmer from Diourbel, Senegal, sold a horse, several cows and a horse cart for about USD 4,500 (about 5.5 lakh taka) by October 2023 and, with loans from relatives, spent more than USD 10,000 (about 12 lakh 21 thousand taka) in total to come to the United States.

Mohamed surrendered to Border Patrol agents in Arizona, who held him for one night and then released him; in New York he stayed at a migrant shelter near Times Square and was expelled within a month after another migrant complained that he had entered the women's toilet (he said by mistake, unable to read the sign); he then slept on the '2 train' subway.

Mohamed said he had no idea that climate disasters such as drought and flood would carry very little weight in his US asylum application, although he cited the climate disaster that destroyed his livelihood as the reason for migrating.

In recent months at least half a dozen WhatsApp groups linking several thousand West African migrants have formed in New York, working as support groups where members share job and room-rent information; migrants also wait outside a local Home Depot hoping to be called for odd jobs.

Griselda from Quetzaltenango, Guatemala mortgaged her father's land for a loan and, with a broker's help, travelled three weeks with two children to the US-Mexico border in 2018; in Texas US officials asked for the children's birth certificates and took them to a migrant shelter, and her husband later sent bus tickets to New York.

CJI and Documented analysed more than 9 million US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) apprehension records for 2010-2024, obtained by public-records request by University of Virginia researchers and CJI, which include birthplace; about 35 percent of records have the birthplace field blank, and CBP officers usually cannot speak migrants' languages so place names are often misspelt.

The investigation's final list of climate-hit origin areas with above-average migration to the US southern border contains 15 areas in Bangladesh, 96 in Senegal and 683 in Guatemala; about 55 countries with above-average migration were hit by three or more natural disasters in 2019-2024 according to the EM-DAT disaster database.
facts.source_in_article: Columbia Journalism Investigations (CJI) and Documented analysis

facts.statement: More than 1,800 Senegalese migrants from western and central Senegal crossed the US-Mexico border between 2019 and 2024, from practically zero before.
facts.source_in_article: Columbia Journalism Investigations (CJI) and Documented analysis

facts.statement: EM-DAT disaster data show about 300 people died in floods in Feni and surrounding areas in the last 10 years; Feni has 16 lakh residents.

Dhaka University geographer and disaster expert Sanjida Murshed said rising sea level due to climate change has worsened floods over the last two decades and cut food production in coastal areas like Feni because floodwater has nowhere to drain.

The Bronx imam Sheikh Tidiane Ndao said news of the threats facing migrants in the United States has not yet reached Senegal; he still gets more than 10 phone calls a month from Senegalese farmers seeking help, drawn by the lure of earning more in a week in the US than in several months in Senegal.

About 14 crore 30 lakh (143 million) people from low-income countries of the global South may be forced to leave their homes by 2050 because of climate change, with Latin America, South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa most affected.
facts.source_in_article: CJI and Documented report (source not named)

headline_en: Cost of sending remittances from Saudi Arabia is high and can be cut: Governor
summary_en: At the opening of the Saudi Arabia-Bangladesh Business Summit in Banani, Dhaka on 7 October 2025, Bangladesh Bank Governor Ahsan H. Mansur said workers pay 6 to 10 percent to send remittances from Saudi Arabia and that the two countries' financial sectors could cut this cost. Other speakers discussed investment, exporting skilled nurses and workers, and the low share of skilled workers among about 21 lakh Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia.

facts.statement: Bangladesh Bank Governor Ahsan H. Mansur said expatriates in Saudi Arabia pay between 6 and 10 percent in costs to send their remittances to Bangladesh, which he called a huge burden on them.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank Governor Ahsan H. Mansur

facts.statement: The Bangladesh Bank Governor said the cost of sending remittances from Saudi Arabia is comparatively much higher, and that a more efficient, lower-cost money transfer system is needed; financial institutions, central banks and related agencies of the two countries can work together on it.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank Governor Ahsan H. Mansur

facts.statement: The Bangladesh Bank Governor said Saudi Arabia is the biggest source of remittances to Bangladesh and also the biggest source of its foreign currency inflow.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank Governor Ahsan H. Mansur

facts.statement: The Governor said Bangladesh wants the lives of Bangladeshi workers in Saudi Arabia to improve and their incomes to rise, and that work is needed on trade, the economy, the financial transaction system and labour-market development between the two countries; some problems exist but can be solved.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank Governor Ahsan H. Mansur

facts.statement: About 21 lakh Bangladeshis currently work in Saudi Arabia, but only 22 percent of them are skilled workers; joint initiatives with Saudi training and educational institutions could raise this rate.
facts.source_in_article: Masrur Reaz, chairman of private research body Policy Exchange, in a paper at the summit

facts.statement: BNP standing committee member Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury said the remittance now coming from Saudi Arabia is commendable but could grow many times over if skill development programmes are taken up.
facts.source_in_article: Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury, BNP standing committee member

facts.statement: Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury said former president Ziaur Rahman first took the initiative to sign government-level agreements to send workers, which formally began the sending of workers from Bangladesh to Middle Eastern countries; before that workers went in a scattered way through private initiative.

The Saudi Arabia Bangladesh Chamber of Commerce and Industry (SABCCI), which organised the summit, said no joint business chamber had existed between the two countries in 53 years until now, and that it can now work to increase exports from Bangladesh including skilled nurses and workers.

headline_en: More than USD 2.5 billion in remittances came in September
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank sources say expatriates sent USD 268 crore 58 lakh in September 2025, USD 16.5 crore more than in August. The article gives comparison figures and the reasons cited for continued growth.

facts.statement: Expatriates sent USD 268 crore 58 lakh in remittances in September 2025, which is USD 16.5 crore more than the previous month.
In the first 21 days of September 2025 expatriates sent USD 203 crore 10 lakh; in the same period of the previous year the amount was USD 163 crore 40 lakh.
Remittances were USD 242 crore 18 lakh in August 2025 and USD 240 crore 41 lakh in September 2024.

Bank officials say remittance inflow through legal channels has risen since the fall of the Awami League government in August 2024 and the high dollar price also encourages sending by the legal route.
March 2025 holds the single-month remittance record at USD 329 crore; no month since has passed USD 300 crore (as of early October 2025).
Reasons given for higher remittances: illegal hundi business has shrunk as money laundering fell, and the dollar exchange rate in the banking channel is stable.

key_quote_bn: বিদায়ী সেপ্টেম্বর মাসে প্রবাসীরা ২৬৮ কোটি ৫৮ লাখ ডলারের প্রবাসী আয় পাঠিয়েছেন, যা আগের মাসের চেয়ে সাড়ে ১৬ কোটি ডলার বেশি।

headline_en: Krishi Bank is now third in collecting remittances
summary_en: Bangladesh Krishi Bank rose to third place among banks collecting remittances in January-August 2025, from 15th in 2023 and seventh in 2024. The article lists the top five banks, their volumes, and how Krishi Bank now delivers remittances through bKash, Nagad and exchange houses so recipients need not visit a branch.

facts.statement: Krishi Bank ranked third among banks in collecting remittances in the first eight months of 2025, collecting USD 197 crore 62 lakh, about 9.25 percent of all remittances that came to Bangladesh in that period.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank report; Krishi Bank sources

facts.statement: State-owned Krishi Bank was 15th in remittance collection in 2023, rose eight places to seventh in 2024, and is third so far in 2025.
Krishi Bank collected USD 11 crore 60 lakh in remittances in January 2025 and USD 30 crore 19 lakh in August 2025.
Total remittances to Bangladesh in January-August 2025 were USD 21.45 billion (USD 2,145 crore).

Around 2018 Krishi Bank received only USD 5 to 7 lakh in remittances a month; it began building remittance capacity from 2018 by working with the world's large remittance-collecting companies and pushing branches that collected none.
facts.source_in_article: Ali Hossain Prodhania, Krishi Bank chairman 2018-2021 (now BIBM supernumerary professor and NRBC Bank chairman)

facts.statement: The top five banks brought 49 percent of remittances in January-August 2025: in order Islami Bank, Agrani Bank, Krishi Bank, Janata Bank and BRAC Bank. Together they brought USD 10.5 billion (USD 1,050 crore) of the USD 21.45 billion total.
The three state-owned banks in the top five (Krishi, Agrani, Janata) brought USD 5.46 billion (USD 546 crore), 25 percent of all remittances in January-August 2025.
Sonali Bank was second in remittance collection in January 2025 with USD 17 crore 93 lakh but fell to seventh in August 2025 with USD 11 crore 75 lakh.

Krishi Bank has more than one thousand branches spread across remote areas. Previously recipients had to come to the bank to collect remittances; now, through agreements with MFS companies including bKash and Nagad and with money exchange houses, customers get the service at home.
facts.source_in_article: Mostafizur Rahman, General Manager, Krishi Bank

facts.statement: BRAC Bank was third in January 2025 with USD 16 crore 27 lakh in remittances and fell to fifth in August 2025 with USD 15 crore 87 lakh.

Islami Bank has consistently held first place in remittance collection: USD 28 crore 23 lakh in January 2025 and USD 55 crore 58 lakh in August 2025. Bankers say Islami Bank's presence in the Middle East and other countries with many Bangladeshi workers is better than any other bank's.

Remittances were USD 242 crore 20 lakh in August 2025 against USD 222 crore 41 lakh in August 2024, growth of about 9 percent; banking was disrupted in the first week of August 2024 by the student-public movement and change of government.

Bankers say the government's tough steps against sending money by illegal routes and the government incentive for sending by legal routes are playing a big role in remittance growth, and that the dollar crisis has largely eased.

headline_en: Technology-driven planning needed to raise remittances
summary_en: At a bKash-organised workshop on Bangladesh's changing remittance landscape at Bhawal Resort, Gazipur on 25 September 2025, bank and fintech officials said remittance sending has become faster through MFS, money transfer companies and digital platforms, and that AI, blockchain and stablecoins could increase legal inflows. Speakers gave figures on the diaspora, skills, digital share and smartphone use.

facts.statement: More than 1.5 crore Bangladeshi expatriates send income home each year; about 1.5 crore Bangladeshis are in 176 countries of the world.
facts.source_in_article: workshop speakers; Mohammad Zahidul Ahsan, head of remittance, bKash commercial division

facts.statement: More than 50 percent of Bangladeshi workers abroad are still unskilled, so remittance inflow is not rising at the expected rate.

About 70 percent of remittances to Bangladesh now come through digital channels, though demand for cash remittance has not completely gone; earlier remittance meant 'cash over the counter' collected at a distant bank branch or NGO office, costing more time and money.

bKash's chief commercial officer said bank representatives used to go abroad to increase workers' accounts and transactions, but now the whole process of sending remittances through MFS and money transfer companies has become digital.
facts.source_in_article: Ali Ahmed, Chief Commercial Officer, bKash

facts.statement: 92 percent of remittance-dependent households in Bangladesh now use a smartphone, and 77 percent of them are connected to the internet.
facts.source_in_article: Joyanta Sen, General Manager, marketing, bKash

facts.statement: Trust Bank's head of treasury said supervision and policy decisions sometimes negatively affect banks' remittance receipts.
facts.source_in_article: Zahurul Karim Chowdhury, head of treasury, Trust Bank

facts.statement: Speakers said modernising remittance sending with artificial intelligence, blockchain and stablecoins would increase remittances through legal channels; Taptap Send's head of growth said people now want to send money fast and easily.
facts.source_in_article: workshop speakers; Sudarshan Shubhashish Das, Head of Growth, Taptap Send

headline_en: Three held captive by traffickers in deep hills rescued, one detained
summary_en: BGB rescued three men from Ramu, Cox's Bazar who were held captive by a human-trafficking gang in the deep hills of Baraitali, Teknaf on the night of 25 September 2025, and detained a Rohingya youth. The men had been lured with a promise of being taken to Malaysia by sea via Thailand and were being held for ransom. The article lists four other anti-trafficking operations in Teknaf in September 2025.

facts.statement: BGB rescued three people held captive by a human-trafficking gang from the deep hills of the Baraitali area of Teknaf upazila, Cox's Bazar at about 9 pm on Thursday 25 September 2025, and detained a Rohingya youth, Md. Sadek (25), a resident of Jamtoli refugee camp in Ukhiya, on charges of involvement in trafficking.

The three rescued men were taken into the hills of Teknaf with the lure of being taken to Malaysia by sea via Thailand; the traffickers then tried to extract ransom from their families and threatened to sell them to a trafficking group based in Malaysia if ransom was not paid.
The three rescued men and the detained Rohingya youth were handed over to Teknaf police station; the BGB commander said action would be taken against them under the prevailing law.
facts.source_in_article: Lt Col Ashikur Rahman, commander, Teknaf-2 BGB Battalion

facts.statement: In September 2025 alone, law-enforcement operations in Teknaf detained members of trafficking gangs at least five times.
On Tuesday 23 September 2025 the Coast Guard rescued five abducted people from the deep hills of Kachchhapia, Baharchhara, Teknaf and detained two members of a human-trafficking gang.
On Monday 22 September 2025 a RAB and BGB operation in Teknaf detained three people with weapons and rescued 84 victims.
On 18 September 2025 the Coast Guard rescued 66 people in Teknaf (in an anti-trafficking operation).
On 16 September 2025 BGB detained 12 members of human-trafficking gangs and rescued 11 victims in Teknaf.

headline_en: The government must take strong steps
summary_en: A Prothom Alo editorial says Cox's Bazar has become a regular sea route for human trafficking to Malaysia, mainly of Rohingya but also of Bangladeshi youths lured onto the unsafe route, and that traffickers become active when the sea calms after the monsoon and before winter. It cites 21 departure points, more than 657 Rohingya deaths at sea in 2024, and obstacles to prosecution, and calls for trawler tracking, faster trials and coordinated enforcement.

facts.statement: Cox's Bazar has become a regular route for human trafficking by sea in recent years; trafficking by sea takes place through 21 points in Teknaf, Ukhiya, Maheshkhali, Cox's Bazar Sadar and other upazilas of the district.
Trafficking gangs become active in the period after the monsoon winds leave and before winter starts, when the sea is calm.
Because the Cox's Bazar sea route has become regular, traffickers are also luring a section of Bangladeshi youths to cross the sea to Malaysia on this unsafe route.

More than 657 Rohingya died on dangerous sea journeys in 2024; deaths in the jungles of Thailand on the way to Malaysia, torture by traffickers and deaths when food and water ran out on trawlers have been reported at various times in international media.
The editorial says human trafficking is having a negative effect on Bangladesh's labour market in Malaysia and elsewhere in South-East Asia.

Cox's Bazar's Superintendent of Police said Rohingya girl children are the most trafficked, that victims are regularly rescued and traffickers arrested in joint-force operations, and that the number trafficked has fallen; the editorial questions how credible this claim is.
facts.source_in_article: Cox's Bazar Superintendent of Police, quoted in editorial

facts.statement: At a meeting at the Cox's Bazar Superintendent of Police's office on 2 September 2025, law-enforcement agencies, lawyers, journalists and NGO representatives called for advance preparation to stop human trafficking in the winter season.

About five thousand trawlers are engaged in sea fishing off Cox's Bazar and law enforcers have no specific data on which are involved in trafficking; the editorial urges installing GPRS systems on trawlers and bringing boatmen under an online database.
Trafficking cases stall because trafficked Rohingya families are unwilling to file cases, and because of slow case disposal and trial, lack of witnesses and intimidation by offenders.
More than 14 lakh Rohingya, old and new arrivals together, have taken shelter in Cox's Bazar.

headline_en: United States now tops remittance sources; tax announcement raises worry
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank data show the United States was the largest single-country source of remittances to Bangladesh in January-March 2025 (USD 144.49 crore, about 18 percent). President Trump's proposed 5 percent tax on remittances sent by non-citizens from the US has raised concern, though some bankers say the effect would be limited because large exchange houses aggregate remittances from other countries and route them through the US. Country-by-country figures for the quarter are given.

facts.statement: In the January-March 2025 quarter remittances to Bangladesh recorded as coming from the United States were USD 144.49 crore, about 18 percent of the total and the highest of any single country.
Total remittances to Bangladesh in January-March 2025 were USD 801 crore against USD 627 crore a year earlier, growth of about 28 percent.

Remittances to Bangladesh by source country in January-March 2025: UAE about USD 109 crore (second), Saudi Arabia about USD 105 crore, United Kingdom USD 97 crore, Malaysia USD 63 crore, Kuwait USD 46 crore, Oman USD 44 crore, Italy USD 40 crore and Qatar USD 31 crore.
Remittances from the United States were USD 33 crore 7 lakh in April 2025 and USD 427 crore in the first 10 months (July-April) of fiscal year 2024-25.

US President Donald Trump proposed a 5 percent tax on remittances sent from the United States, under the 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' approved in the House Budget Committee. It would apply to remittances sent by all immigrants other than US citizens, including green-card holders and H-1B visa holders, with no minimum threshold, so it would apply to money sent by Bangladeshis too.

facts.statement: Bankers explain that large global remittance companies such as Western Union and MoneyGram buy remittances from small companies in various countries, aggregate them and send them to the destination country from one specific country, which is why the United States rose to the top after August 2024; if the US taxes remittances, some expect the money would again be sent directly from the source countries.

Factors behind remittance growth in January-March 2025 were less use of hundi or informal routes, banks' competitive exchange rates, availability of the incentive, and extra money sent for Eid-ul-Fitr; bankers say the gap between formal and informal dollar rates has narrowed.
